Homework 8: Final Project Data and Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Title: Electric Vehicle Adoption and Charging Infrastructure in Washington State¶

Group Members: Anushka Maddisetty, Hamda Hassan, Hemant Arulijothi, Sravya Murala

Date: November 2026

Research Question¶

Is Washington's public charging network keeping pace with EV growth, and how are income and rurality associated with where the gaps are largest?

Data Sources¶

For our project, we will use the following datasets to explore EV adoption and public charging infrastructure across Washington State.

Core Datasets¶

  1. EV Population Size History by County

    • Source: Washington State Department of Licensing
    • Monthly EV registration data by county, used to track EV growth from 2017 to 2025.

  2. Alternative Fueling Stations

    • Source: U.S. Department of Energy
    • Historical public charging station data from 2017 to 2025, used to compare charging infrastructure growth with EV adoption.

Secondary Datasets¶

  1. Median Household Income (2024)

    • Source: U.S. Census Bureau
    • Used to explore whether income is related to EV adoption and charging availability.

  2. Rural–Urban Continuum Codes (2023)

    • Source: USDA
    • Used to compare charging availability between urban and rural counties.

  3. County Population Estimates (2017–2025)

    • Source: U.S. Census Bureau
    • Used to compare counties of different population sizes fairly.

  4. Washington County Boundaries

    • Source: U.S. Census Bureau
    • Used to create county-level maps and identify which county each charging station belongs to.

Optional Dataset¶

  1. EV Population Data
    • Source: Washington State Department of Licensing
    • Used to explore popular EV brands, models, and vehicle types.

Contents¶

  1. EV Registration History
  2. Charging Stations and County Boundaries
  3. Median Household Income and County Population
  4. Rural Urban Codes and Current EV Population
  5. Visualization Brainstorm
  6. Next Steps

1. EV Registration History¶

For this part, we are using the Electric Vehicle Population Size History by County dataset from the Washington State Department of Licensing. The data comes from data.wa.gov at https://data.wa.gov/d/3d5d-sdqb.

We planned to use data from 2017 to 2025 to see how EV adoption has changed over time and which counties have experienced the most growth. This dataset will help us understand the EV adoption side of our research question before comparing it with public charging infrastructure.

We loaded the raw file first so we could see everything and understand its structure before making any changes.

In [1]:
import pandas as pd, geopandas as gpd

ROOT = "/kaggle/input/datasets/sravyahsri/wa-ev-project/WA_EV_Project"
ev_raw = pd.read_csv(f"{ROOT}/01_Core_Datasets/EV_Registration_History_by_County.csv")
print(ev_raw.shape)
ev_raw.head()

(36913, 10)
Out[1]:
Date County State Vehicle Primary Use Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs) Electric Vehicle (EV) Total Non-Electric Vehicle Total Total Vehicles Percent Electric Vehicles
0 August 31 2023 Ada ID Passenger 4 0 4 218 222 1.80
1 April 30 2023 Lee AL Passenger 1 1 2 23 25 8.00
2 November 30 2024 Hendricks IN Passenger 1 0 1 10 11 9.09
3 December 31 2021 Wahkiakum WA Truck 0 0 0 1820 1820 0.00
4 April 30 2024 Essex MA Passenger 2 0 2 16 18 11.11

Each row is one county in one month for one vehicle use which is either passenger or truck. There are 10 columns. They give the number of battery electric vehicles and plug in hybrids plus the EV total and the non electric total and all vehicles and the percent that are electric. The raw file has 36,913 rows because it covers many states and not only Washington. Three things to watch out for. The file includes other states like Idaho and California. The Date column is text like “August 31 2023” so it has to be converted. And every county appears twice per month because trucks and passenger vehicles are separate.

First we kept only Washington and converted the dates. We dropped 2026 because it is a partial year and our charging data stops at 2025. We kept passenger vehicles only because public chargers are mostly used by passenger cars. Then we matched each county name to its 5 digit FIPS code using the boundary file so it can be merged with the other datasets later.

In [2]:
ev = ev_raw[ev_raw["State"] == "WA"].copy()
ev["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(ev["Date"], format="%B %d %Y")
ev = ev[ev["Date"].dt.year <= 2025]                   
ev = ev[ev["Vehicle Primary Use"] == "Passenger"]     

b = gpd.read_file(f"{ROOT}/03_Geographic_Data/WA_County_Boundaries_2025/WA_County_Boundaries_2025.shp")
ev["fips"] = ev["County"].map(dict(zip(b["NAME"], b["GEOID"])))

ev = ev.rename(columns={
    "Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs)": "bev",
    "Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs)": "phev",
    "Electric Vehicle (EV) Total": "ev_total",
    "Total Vehicles": "total_vehicles",
    "Percent Electric Vehicles": "pct_electric"})
ev["year"], ev["month"] = ev["Date"].dt.year, ev["Date"].dt.month
ev = ev[["fips", "County", "Date", "year", "month", "bev", "phev", "ev_total", "total_vehicles", "pct_electric"]]

# Verifying
print(ev["fips"].isna().sum(), "unmatched counties")
print(ev.duplicated(["fips", "Date"]).sum(), "duplicate county-months")
print(ev["fips"].nunique(), "counties,", ev.shape[0], "rows")   

ev_dec = ev[ev["month"] == 12].copy()
print(ev_dec.shape)                                              

0 unmatched counties
0 duplicate county-months
39 counties, 4212 rows
(351, 10)

The verification is clear. All 39 counties matched a FIPS code and there are no duplicate county months. The final table has 4,212 rows which is 39 counties times 108 months. We also made a December only table with 351 rows since the charging station data is a snapshot from the end of each year.

Summary¶

Adoption is very uneven. In 2025 the average county had about 6,800 EVs but the biggest county had over 133,000 which is about half of the state total. The smallest county had only 5. King County grew from 15,949 EVs in 2017 to 133,180 in 2025 which is 8.4 times more. That is a little slower than the whole state which grew about 9.4 times. So King is huge in raw numbers but it is not the fastest growing county. From 2019 to 2025 the fastest growth among counties that already had at least 100 EVs was in Franklin and Grant and Yakima which grew 9.0 and 8.5 and 8.2 times. We want to explore which counties grew fastest in percent terms and not only in raw numbers. A small county can look like it is booming just because it started from almost nothing. We also want to see how the Puget Sound counties compare with the rest of the state. By Puget Sound counties we mean King and Pierce and Snohomish and Kitsap and Thurston. Some limits to keep in mind. Counties with very few EVs will give noisy ratios later so we will flag them. The data only covers passenger vehicles and December snapshots. It still needs to be merged with charging ports and population and income and the rural urban label before we can answer the main question.

For visuals we are thinking of a line chart of statewide EV growth and a county map of EVs per 1,000 residents and small multiples showing growth by county.

2. Charging Stations and County Boundaries¶

For this part, we are using the Alternative Fueling Stations data from the Department of Energy at https://afdc.energy.gov/data_download. This dataset contains historical data from 2017 to 2025, which we will use to see how charging infrastructure has changed over time and whether it is keeping up with EV growth.

It also uses the Census county boundary file for Washington so every station can be placed in a county. This will help us understand the charging infrastructure side of our research question.

In [11]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import altair as alt
In [12]:
ROOT = "/kaggle/input/datasets/sravyahsri/wa-ev-project/WA_EV_Project"
stations_path = f"{ROOT}/01_Core_Datasets/Charging_Stations_Historical"
boundary_path = f"{ROOT}/03_Geographic_Data/WA_County_Boundaries_2025/WA_County_Boundaries_2025.shp"

Each row is one charging station in one yearly snapshot. The station count grew from 722 in 2017 to 2,792 in 2025. Every station in the files is open and public and has coordinates so no filtering was needed. A few things that we need to check is that there is no county column so counties have to come from a spatial join. The port counts are blank when a station does not have that charger type so we treated blanks as zero. Also a row is a station and not a port. Stations can have many ports so we used ports as the main measure.

In [13]:
frames = []
for year in range(2017, 2026):
  df = pd.read_csv(f'{stations_path}/WA_Charging_Stations_{year}.csv', low_memory=False)
  df['snapshot_year'] = year
  frames.append(df)

stations = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
print(stations.shape)

We turned each station into a point and joined it to the county polygons. Twelve stations did not land inside any county. Nine of them were within a mile of a county border which is probably a coastline issue so we gave them the nearest county. The other three were Walgreens stations from 2019 with coordinates over a thousand miles away so we dropped them. Considering them the nearest county would have put ports in the wrong place.

In [20]:
ev_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    ev,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(ev['Longitude'], ev['Latitude']),
    crs='EPSG:4326'
)

counties = counties.to_crs('EPSG:4326')

ev_gdf = gpd.sjoin(ev_gdf, counties[['GEOID', 'NAME', 'geometry']], how='left', predicate='within')

We summed stations and ports for every county and year. Level 1 ports are kept in their own column but left out of the total because they are slow outlet charging and only 15 of them exist in 2025. So total ports means Level 2 plus DC fast. Counties with no stations in a year get a zero. The final table has 351 rows which is 39 counties times 9 years.

In [23]:
county_ports = (ev_gdf.groupby(['GEOID', 'NAME', 'snapshot_year'])
                .agg(stations=('ID', 'count'),
                     l1_ports=('EV Level1 EVSE Num', 'sum'),
                     l2_ports=('EV Level2 EVSE Num', 'sum'),
                     dcfc_ports=('EV DC Fast Count', 'sum'))
                .reset_index())

# Total
county_ports['total_ports'] = county_ports['l2_ports'] + county_ports['dcfc_ports']

Twenty five county years have zero public ports. Garfield has zero in all nine years so EVs per port cannot be calculated there. We need to either use ports per 1,000 EVs or mark those counties as having no ports. Ferry is interesting because it had 1 port from 2017 to 2020 then 0 from 2021 to 2024 and then 9 in 2025. So stations can be removed from the network and not only added.

This mock up checks how the charger mix differs between metro and nonmetro counties. We used the USDA codes where 1 to 3 is metro. In 2025 about 43 percent of nonmetro ports are DC fast compared with about 24 percent in metro. This probably comes from fast chargers built along highways for travelers and not for local drivers. The chart only shows shares so the final version should add the totals because nonmetro has about 720 ports and metro has about 7,070.

In [30]:
rucc = pd.read_csv(f"{ROOT}/02_Secondary_Datasets/WA_Rural_Urban_Codes_2023.csv", dtype={"FIPS": str})
rucc = rucc[rucc["Attribute"] == "RUCC_2023"].assign(rucc=lambda d: d["Value"].astype(int))
area = dict(zip(rucc["FIPS"], np.where(rucc["rucc"] <= 3, "Metro", "Nonmetro")))

p25 = county_ports[county_ports["year"] == 2025].assign(area_type=lambda d: d["fips"].map(area))
mix = (p25.groupby("area_type")[["l2_ports", "dcfc_ports"]].sum().reset_index()
          .melt(id_vars="area_type", var_name="charger", value_name="ports"))
mix["charger"] = mix["charger"].map({"l2_ports": "Level 2", "dcfc_ports": "DC fast"})
mix["pct"] = mix["ports"] / mix.groupby("area_type")["ports"].transform("sum") * 100
print(mix.round(1))

alt.Chart(mix).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X("area_type:N", title=None, axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    y=alt.Y("pct:Q", stack="zero", title="Share of public ports (%)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 100])),
    color=alt.Color("charger:N", scale=alt.Scale(domain=["Level 2", "DC fast"], range=["#41b6c4", "#7570b3"]), title="Charger type"),
    tooltip=["area_type", "charger", alt.Tooltip("pct:Q", format=".1f"), alt.Tooltip("ports:Q", format=",")]
).properties(width=300, height=300, title=alt.Title("Mock-up: mix of public charger types, 2025"))

Summary¶

The charging network grew a lot but not evenly. Level 2 ports grew about 3.8 times and DC fast ports grew about 10 times between 2017 and 2025 so fast charging is expanding the quickest. Four counties had no DC fast ports in 2025 which are Pacific and Island and Mason and Garfield. We want to compare this growth with EV growth to see if chargers are keeping up. We also want to see whether the counties with the fewest ports are the rural low income ones. Counties on the I-90 and I-5 corridors may have many ports because of travelers and not because of local EV owners so we need to keep that in mind. The limits are that these are year end snapshots and that three stations were dropped for bad coordinates. This table still needs to be merged with EV counts and population and income and the rural urban label.

For visuals we are thinking of a county map of ports per 1,000 EVs and a line chart of Level 2 versus DC fast growth and a ranked bar chart of DC fast access by county.

3. Median Household Income and County Population¶

For this part, we are using two supporting datasets from the U.S. Census Bureau: median household income and county population estimates.

  • Income: American Community Survey, table B19013, at https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B19013.
  • Population: County Population Estimates, at https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/.

We will use these datasets to explore how income is related to EV adoption and charging availability, and to compare counties of different population sizes fairly.

The income file has one row per county plus one extra row at the top that only describes the columns. It has 40 rows and 5 columns before cleaning. The numbers are 5 year ACS estimates for 2020 to 2024 in 2024 dollars and each estimate comes with a margin of error. The last column is empty so it needs to be dropped.

We dropped the description row and the empty column and renamed the columns. The GEO ID looks like 0500000US53033 so we kept the last five characters to get the county FIPS code. We also removed the words County and Washington from the names so they match the other files. After cleaning there are 39 rows and 39 unique FIPS codes with no missing values.

In [33]:
income = (income_raw
          .drop(index=0)                                  
          .drop(columns=[c for c in income_raw.columns if c.startswith("Unnamed")])
          .rename(columns={"B19013_001E": "median_income", "B19013_001M": "income_moe"}))
income["median_income"] = pd.to_numeric(income["median_income"])
income["income_moe"] = pd.to_numeric(income["income_moe"])
income["fips"] = income["GEO_ID"].str[-5:]                 
income["county"] = income["NAME"].str.replace(" County, Washington", "", regex=False)
income = income[["fips", "county", "median_income", "income_moe"]].reset_index(drop=True)

print("rows:", len(income), "| unique FIPS:", income.fips.nunique(), "| missing values:", int(income.isna().sum().sum()))
print("all FIPS start with 53 (Washington):", income.fips.str.startswith("53").all())
income.sample(5, random_state=1)

Income here is a survey estimate and not an exact count. We turned the 90 percent margin of error into a standard error and then into a percent of the estimate. Most counties are under 5 percent but small counties are much less reliable. Garfield is the worst at 13 percent then Wahkiakum at 9.8 percent and Pend Oreille at 7 percent. We also split the counties into four income groups with about the same number of counties in each.

In [34]:
income["income_se"] = income["income_moe"] / 1.645
income["income_cv_pct"] = income["income_se"] / income["median_income"] * 100
income["income_low"] = income["median_income"] - income["income_moe"]
income["income_high"] = income["median_income"] + income["income_moe"]
income["income_quartile"] = pd.qcut(income["median_income"], 4,
                                    labels=["Q1 (lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (highest)"])

print(income[["median_income", "income_moe", "income_cv_pct"]].describe().round(1))
print("\nleast reliable estimates:")
print(income.nlargest(3, "income_cv_pct")[["county", "median_income", "income_moe", "income_cv_pct"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))

To combine the two files we made a five digit FIPS code from the state and county numbers. In the first file the year codes 9 and 10 and 11 are July 2017 and 2018 and 2019 and code 12 is the April 2020 census count. We checked this by comparing code 12 with the 2020 base in the second file and the biggest difference in any county was 2,201 people. After stacking there are 351 rows which is 39 counties times 9 years with no missing values or duplicates. One thing we had to look for is that the two files come from different Census releases so there could be a small jump at 2020. Also population is for July 1 but EV registrations are for December 31.

In [37]:
def make_fips(df):
    return df["STATE"].astype(str).str.zfill(2) + df["COUNTY"].astype(str).str.zfill(3)

YEAR_CODE = {9: 2017, 10: 2018, 11: 2019}
a = pop_a[pop_a["AGEGRP"] == 0].copy()
a["fips"] = make_fips(a)
census_2020 = a[a["YEAR"] == 12].set_index("fips")["TOT_POP"]
a = a[a["YEAR"].isin(YEAR_CODE)].assign(year=lambda d: d["YEAR"].map(YEAR_CODE))
a = a[["fips", "year", "TOT_POP"]].rename(columns={"TOT_POP": "population"})

b = pop_b[pop_b["SUMLEV"] == 50].copy()
b["fips"] = make_fips(b)
base_2020 = b.set_index("fips")["ESTIMATESBASE2020"]
year_cols = [f"POPESTIMATE{y}" for y in range(2020, 2026)]
b = b.melt(id_vars="fips", value_vars=year_cols, var_name="year", value_name="population")
b["year"] = b["year"].str[-4:].astype(int)

# checking the YEAR code
diff = (census_2020 - base_2020).abs()
print(f"YEAR code 12 vs Vintage 2025 April-2020 base: largest county difference = {diff.max():,} people")

population = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True).sort_values(["fips", "year"]).reset_index(drop=True)
population = population.merge(income[["fips", "county"]], on="fips", how="left")
print("rows:", len(population), "(39 counties x 9 years =", 39 * 9, ")")
print("missing values:", int(population.isna().sum().sum()), "| duplicate county-years:", int(population.duplicated(["fips", "year"]).sum()))
print("years:", sorted(population.year.unique()))
population.head(10)

The correlation between income and population growth is about minus 0.03 which is basically zero. So growth between 2017 and 2025 is not tied to income. The fastest growing counties are small nonmetro ones like Wahkiakum and Lincoln and Mason which grew between 14 and 17 percent while Whitman barely grew at 0.4 percent.

Now we bring in the EV registrations. We kept Washington passenger vehicles only and the December snapshot of each year to match the charging station data. Merging with population and income gives a county year table with EVs per 1,000 residents. Every county year found an EV match. In 2025 San Juan has the highest EVs per 1,000 residents at 65.5 followed by King at 56.8 and Jefferson at 41.2.

In [48]:
ev = pd.read_csv(PATHS["ev"])
ev = ev[ev["State"] == "WA"].copy()
ev = ev[ev["Vehicle Primary Use"] == "Passenger"]      
ev["date"] = pd.to_datetime(ev["Date"], format="%B %d %Y")
ev = ev[(ev["date"].dt.month == 12) & ev["date"].dt.year.between(2017, 2025)]
ev = (ev.assign(year=ev["date"].dt.year)
        .groupby(["County", "year"], as_index=False)["Electric Vehicle (EV) Total"].sum()
        .rename(columns={"County": "county", "Electric Vehicle (EV) Total": "evs"}))

panel = (population.merge(ev, on=["county", "year"], how="left")
                   .merge(county[["fips", "median_income", "income_quartile", "area_type"]], on="fips"))
print("county-years without an EV match:", int(panel["evs"].isna().sum()))
panel["evs_per_1000"] = panel["evs"] / panel["population"] * 1000
panel.to_csv("clean/panel_ev_pop_income.csv", index=False)
panel.query("year == 2025").nlargest(5, "evs_per_1000")[["county", "evs", "population", "evs_per_1000", "median_income"]].round(1)

To see this over time we grouped the counties into the four income groups and added up their EVs and populations. All groups grow but the highest income group grows much faster. The top line is mostly King County because King is so big so we should not describe it as all rich counties.

In [51]:

    subtitle="Mock-up: EVs per 1,000 residents by county income quartile, Dec 31 each year"))
Out[51]:

The gap between the highest and lowest income groups grew from 3.9 EVs per 1,000 residents in 2017 to 30.6 in 2025. But the ratio between them fell from 5.8 times to 4.1 times. So the gap is getting bigger in absolute terms while the lower income counties are slowly catching up in relative terms.

Summary¶

Income and population are what let us compare counties fairly. Income varies a lot from about 55,000 dollars in Whitman to about 125,000 dollars in King and it is higher in metro counties on average. Population is very uneven too with King and Pierce and Snohomish holding 52 percent of the state. In 2025 higher income counties have more EVs per resident with a correlation of 0.69 and the gap between income groups is growing in absolute terms. What we still need is the charging port counts so we can see if chargers follow the same pattern. The limits are that income is a five year estimate with large margins of error in small counties and that population is a July estimate while EVs and chargers are December counts.

For visuals we want the income scatter with ports per 1,000 EVs on the y axis and the income group line chart using ports instead of EVs. We also want a map of county income next to a map of charging gaps.

4. Rural Urban Codes and Current EV Population¶

For this part, we are using USDA Rural Urban Continuum Codes from https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-continuum-codes and the Washington DOL EV Population data from https://data.wa.gov/d/f6w7-q2d2.

We will use the rural–urban codes to compare EV adoption and charging availability between urban and rural counties.

The EV Population Data is an optional dataset that we can use to explore popular EV brands, models, and vehicle types across Washington.

We turned the long table into one row per county. The codes run from 1 to 9 where 1 is the biggest metro areas and 9 is the most rural. We called counties with codes 1 to 3 metro and 4 to 9 nonmetro. We also made a three level version that splits nonmetro counties into adjacent and not adjacent to a metro area using the description text.

In [56]:
rucc = (rucc_raw.pivot(index=["FIPS", "County_Name"], columns="Attribute", values="Value")
                .rename_axis(columns=None)
                .reset_index()
                .rename(columns={"FIPS": "fips", "County_Name": "county_full", "Description": "rucc_description",
                                 "RUCC_2023": "rucc", "Population_2020": "rucc_pop_2020"}))
rucc["county"] = rucc["county_full"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)
rucc["rucc"] = rucc["rucc"].astype(int)
rucc["rucc_pop_2020"] = rucc["rucc_pop_2020"].astype(int)

rucc["area_type"] = np.where(rucc["rucc"] <= 3, "Metro", "Nonmetro")
rucc["adjacency"] = np.select(
    [rucc["rucc"] <= 3, rucc["rucc_description"].str.contains("not adjacent", case=False)],
    ["Metro", "Nonmetro, not adjacent"], default="Nonmetro, adjacent")

rucc = rucc[["fips", "county", "rucc", "area_type", "adjacency", "rucc_description", "rucc_pop_2020"]]
rucc.head()

The table has 39 rows with no duplicates and no missing values. There are 19 metro and 20 nonmetro counties. Among the nonmetro ones 15 are next to a metro area and 5 are not. One thing we had to check is whether metro includes some very rural counties like Stevens and Skamania because they are part of a larger metro area. So metro and nonmetro is a rough split and the full 1 to 9 code or the adjacency version may work better in some charts.

The file has two vehicle types. About 241,840 are battery electric and 58,302 are plug in hybrids. The electric range is 0 for 65.7 percent of the rows. That does not mean the car has no range. It means the range was never researched so we will treat those zeros as missing. The only column with missing values is legislative district at 0.3 percent and the model years run from 1999 to 2027.

We kept only Washington rows which dropped 789 rows from other states. We renamed the columns and shortened the vehicle type to BEV and PHEV and turned the zero ranges into missing values. There are no duplicate vehicle IDs.

Metro counties have 281,595 EVs and nonmetro counties have 17,758. Battery electric vehicles are 81 percent of EVs in metro counties and 74 percent in nonmetro counties. Tesla is 41 percent of metro EVs but 31 percent of nonmetro EVs while Chevrolet and Ford and Nissan are more common in nonmetro counties. The median range is about the same at 44 and 42 miles but it only uses the cars where range is known so we would not make it a main result.

We made a county summary with the number of EVs and the BEV share and the median range and the median model year. We saved it with the clean RUCC table for the group.

In [65]:
import os
os.makedirs("clean", exist_ok=True)

evpop_county = (evpop.groupby("fips")
                .agg(evs_now=("ev_type", "size"),
                     bev_share_pct=("ev_type", lambda s: (s == "BEV").mean() * 100),
                     median_range_mi=("range_mi", "median"),
                     median_model_year=("model_year", "median"))
                .reset_index())

rucc.to_csv("clean/rucc_clean.csv", index=False)
evpop_county.to_csv("clean/evpop_county_summary.csv", index=False)

        .rename(columns={"County": "county", "Electric Vehicle (EV) Total": "evs"})[["county", "evs"]])

Summary¶

The rural urban codes give us the rural side of our question. The metro and nonmetro split is almost even with 19 and 20 counties but metro includes some rural counties so we want to also try the adjacency version and the full 1 to 9 code. The EV population file shows that metro and nonmetro counties are a bit different. Nonmetro EVs are more often plug in hybrids and less often Tesla. What we still need is to join the codes with the charging ports so we can see if nonmetro counties have fewer ports per EV. The limits are that the EV population file is a newer snapshot than the December counts and that electric range is missing for most vehicles.

For visuals we want a map of rural urban type next to a map of charging gaps and a dot plot of ports per 1,000 EVs by county type and a chart of BEV share by county type.

5. Visualization Brainstorm¶

Our question is whether Washington's public charging network is keeping pace with EV growth and whether income and rurality are associated with where the gaps are largest. Every chart uses county level data for 2017 to 2025. We use the same colors everywhere. Blue means metro and orange means nonmetro. Level 2 and DC fast chargers use teal and purple so they never look like metro and nonmetro. Maps use one sequential color scale and gray for counties with too little data.

1. Are chargers growing as fast as EVs?¶

Question: Did public charging ports grow as fast as registered EVs between 2017 and 2025?

Variables: year and statewide EV total and total ports and DC fast ports. The new variable is each series divided by its 2017 value so all lines start at 1.

Encodings: x is year and y is the index and color is the series.

Chart type: Line chart with three lines.

Design: Label the lines directly and add a horizontal line at 1. From our data EVs grew about 9.4 times and total ports about 4.6 times and DC fast ports about 10 times so the lines should separate clearly. We would try a log y scale if the EV line dominates.

2. Where are the biggest charging gaps?¶

Question: Which counties have the fewest public ports for the EVs they have?

Variables: county FIPS and 2025 total ports and 2025 EV total and the county boundary shapes. The new variable is ports per 1,000 EVs. We filter or flag counties with fewer than 500 EVs.

Encodings: Geographic shape is the county and color is ports per 1,000 EVs.

Chart type: Choropleth map made with the Altair geoshape mark.

Design: One sequential color scale with a light color for low values so gaps stand out and gray with a legend note for counties with fewer than 500 EVs. The tooltip shows county and EVs and ports. The title should state the finding.

3. Which counties have the most EVs per fast charger?¶

Question: In which counties does each DC fast port serve the most EVs?

Variables: county and 2025 DC fast ports and 2025 EV total. The new variable is EVs per DC fast port. Counties with zero DC fast ports are listed separately because the ratio cannot be calculated.

Encodings: y is county sorted by the ratio and x is EVs per DC fast port and color is metro or nonmetro.

Chart type: Horizontal ranked bar chart of the top 15 counties.

Design: Blue and orange for the area type and values labeled at the end of each bar. A short note under the chart names the counties with no DC fast ports. Highway counties on I-90 may look better than they are for local drivers so the subtitle should say that.

4. Which counties have high adoption but few chargers?¶

Question: Where is EV adoption high while charging access is low?

Variables: EVs per 1,000 residents and ports per 1,000 EVs for 2025 and county population and area type. The new variables are both ratios.

Encodings: x is EVs per 1,000 residents and y is ports per 1,000 EVs and size is population and color is metro or nonmetro.

Chart type: Scatter plot split into four quadrants.

Design: Dashed lines at the statewide medians and a light label on the high adoption and low ports corner. We label only the outliers such as King and San Juan and Jefferson. We use a log scale on y if a few counties stretch the axis.

5. Do lower income counties have fewer ports per EV?¶

Question: Is county median income related to how many public ports there are per EV?

Variables: Median household income and its margin of error and ports per 1,000 EVs in 2025 and area type and population.

Encodings: x is median income and y is ports per 1,000 EVs and color is metro or nonmetro and size is population.

Chart type: Scatter plot with a trend line. This builds on the income scatter mock up in section 3 by swapping EVs per 1,000 residents for ports per 1,000 EVs.

Design: Start the income axis near 55,000 dollars and format ticks as dollars. Add the correlation to the subtitle and mention that small counties have wide margins of error.

6. Is the gap different in metro and nonmetro counties over time?¶

Question: Has the number of ports per 1,000 EVs changed differently in metro and nonmetro counties since 2017?

Variables: year and area type and total ports and EV total summed by area type. The new variable is ports per 1,000 EVs for each group and year.

Encodings: x is year and y is ports per 1,000 EVs and color is metro or nonmetro.

Chart type: Line chart with two lines. A faint dot for each county could be added behind the lines.

Design: Blue and orange again and direct labels instead of a legend. This builds on the metro and nonmetro mock up in section 4.

6. Next Steps¶

The next step is to merge everything into one table with one row per county per year from 2017 to 2025. We will join the clean files we saved above on the county FIPS code and the year. These are the EV counts by county and year and the charging ports by county and year and the population and income table and the rural urban codes. Then we will calculate EVs per public charging port and ports per 1,000 EVs and EVs per 1,000 residents. We will check for missing values and duplicates and counties with zero ports. Counties like Garfield with no ports and counties with fewer than 500 EVs will be flagged so the ratios do not mislead us. After that we will build the final visualizations and the project website.
